pedagogy.summary: This is the step up from knowing individual angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, on a straight line 180°, vertically opposite are equal) to CHAINING them across a single diagram to find several unknowns, and to setting up and solving an EQUATION for an unknown. Best taught by insisting that every step names the fact that licenses it (reasoning from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks), by keeping the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point), and by holding apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL, adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY. Diagrams are given not-to-scale so pupils must deduce rather than measure.
bestPractices: Require a named reason for every step ('angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' style mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises, tricks don't
Name the WHOLE before calculating: a straight line is a half-turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°); the unknown is the whole minus the known parts
Teach the crossing-lines diagram as two facts held apart — opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary — one diagram, two relationships
Present diagrams NOT to scale so pupils cannot measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts
Progress to letting an unknown be a letter and writing an equation (e.g. 2x+10 = 130 for a vertically opposite pair), linking angle facts to algebra
Build multi-step problems where one found angle becomes the input to the next, and ask pupils to carry the value forward onto the diagram
keyRepresentations: Crossing-lines ('hinged sticks') diagram for vertically-opposite versus adjacent angles
The whole as a fixed total shared among parts — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point
Not-to-scale multi-angle diagrams that force deduction over measurement
An equation written from the diagram (known + unknown = whole; or an opposite pair set equal)
commonMisconceptions: Treating vertically opposite angles as supplementary (subtracting from 180 to find the opposite angle)
Over-generalising that all four angles at a crossing are equal
Using the wrong whole — 360° where 180° applies, or vice versa
Measuring or reading the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing from facts

learn.summary: Pupils (age 11+) move from knowing isolated angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal) to CHAINING those facts across a single not-to-scale diagram to find several unknowns, and to writing and solving an equation for an unknown angle. The core discipline: name the fact that licenses every step (reason from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks or from F/Z mnemonics), keep the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point) for line/point calculations, and hold apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL (found by equality, not subtraction), adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.

activities.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
feedback: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles equal — found by equality, not by subtracting); each adjacent angle is 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so 180−130). Check: 130 + 50 + 130 + 50 = 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°.
For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120 and x = 60.
If you gave 50° for the angle vertically OPPOSITE 130°, you treated an opposite pair as supplementary — opposite angles are equal; it is the ADJACENT angle that is 180−130 = 50°.
If you used 360° for an angle on a straight line (or 180° at a point), you named the wrong whole — a straight line is 180°, a full point is 360°; sanity-check the answer against that total.
If you found the first angle but stalled, write it onto the diagram and use it as the given for the next step — the facts are sound, the chain just needs the value carried forward.
activities.rationale: The objective is multi-step deduction and justification, so the task must require an actual chain where each found angle becomes an input and a named reason is stated at every step; a not-to-scale figure means measuring is unreliable so pupils must deduce from facts, and part (c) links angle facts to setting up and solving an equation.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
Pupils should apply the properties of angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
Angle measure is additive: a whole angle decomposed into parts is the sum of the parts, and unknown angles are found by writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown
learnerActions: Work from a not-to-scale diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, and a third ray splitting the opposite angle into two parts, one marked 40°.

(a) Find the three unmarked angles at the crossing. For each, write the exact fact you used (e.g. 'vertically opposite angles are equal', 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'). Then check that the four angles at the crossing total 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
(b) Find the remaining part of the split angle, carrying the already-found angle forward as a given.
(c) Two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130°; write an equation and solve it for x.

Before calculating, name which relationship applies: for an angle on a line or at a point, say the WHOLE (a straight line is a half-turn 180°, a point is a whole turn 360°) and take the unknown as the whole minus the known parts; but for a vertically opposite angle the unknown is simply EQUAL to its given partner, NOT whole-minus-parts.
Write each found angle onto the diagram so it becomes a visible given for the next step.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are deduced by combining named facts in a chain, where one result feeds the next; a vertically opposite angle is found by equality while line/point unknowns are found by subtracting from the whole, and the not-to-scale picture cannot be measured, so only the facts license the answer.

activities.title: Hinged sticks: why opposite is equal and adjacent is supplementary
feedback: If you expected all four angles to be equal, look at a wide, non-perpendicular crossing: two clearly larger angles and two clearly smaller, with each large–small pair summing to 180°.
If you subtracted the given from 180 to get the OPPOSITE angle, the hinge shows the opposite angle grows with the original — equal, not supplementary.
The opposite pair being equal and each adjacent pair summing to 180° are consistent: 130° + 50° = 180° on each side, and the two 130°s face each other.
activities.rationale: The dynamic hinge gives a direct counterexample to the dominant misconception (treating vertically opposite as supplementary) and to the over-generalisation that all four angles are equal, by letting pupils see opposite angles change together while adjacent angles trade off.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Model a crossing with two hinged sticks (or two rulers pinned at a point).

Open the crossing wider and watch the angle you are opening and the one directly opposite it: observe that they grow TOGETHER and appear to stay equal (the hinge illustrates this; the straight-line facts explain why they must be exactly equal).
At the same time watch an adjacent angle: as one opens the neighbour shrinks, and each adjacent pair still sums to 180°.
State in words why the two opposite angles must be equal, and why an opposite pair cannot both be found by 'take it from 180'.
Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different, to check that NOT all four angles are equal — only opposite pairs are.
Optional screen version: drag one ray so the linked opposite angle updates equal in real time while the adjacent value updates to keep the pair summing to 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: At a crossing there are two distinct relationships held apart: vertically opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary — they cannot both be 'subtract from 180'.

activities.title: Introducing the vocabulary on a labelled crossing
feedback: Opposite pairs: equal. Adjacent pairs along either straight line: sum to 180°.
A tap-reveal confirms the name of a relationship but does not set or check a solved problem; once the vocabulary is secure, move to the chaining task to practise applying it.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal diagram efficiently introduces the naming of relationships; it is a vocabulary scaffold and does not itself require solving or chaining, so it should precede, not replace, the multi-step task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, identify the vertically opposite pair and state the relationship: equal.
Identify an adjacent pair and state the relationship: sum to 180°.
Where available as a reveal, tap an opposite pair to confirm 'equal' and an adjacent pair to confirm 'sum to 180°'.
Name each of the four angles and say which relationship each neighbour has to it.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary — vertically opposite (equal) versus adjacent (supplementary) — is attached to the right pairs on a crossing before any multi-step problem is attempted.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the supplementary-for-opposite trap and match steps to reasons
feedback: For the opposite angle, the correct option equals the given angle; the 180−x option is the supplementary (adjacent) value and is the common error.
A step is only justified when paired with the named fact that licenses it; 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' labels do not count as reasons.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and matching items efficiently probe the key misconception and reason-naming, but they assess isolated facts; they do not require a learner to build and carry a genuine multi-step chain, so they supplement rather than replace the chaining task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Fill in a missing angle given one angle at a crossing or on a straight line.
Answer a multiple-choice item for the angle vertically opposite a given one, where one option is the supplementary value (180−x) — choose the equal value and reject the trap.
Match each found angle in a worked solution to the exact fact that justifies it.
Set a slider or chosen value for one angle and state the resulting opposite and adjacent angles.
activities.intendedInsight: These recognition and matching items are intended to rehearse the equal-versus-supplementary distinction and the habit of naming a reason; they check isolated facts rather than demonstrate a mastered multi-step chain.

constraints: Diagrams must be presented NOT to scale so pupils cannot reliably measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts, and a reminder that the picture is not to scale is appropriate.
Every step must be justified with a named angle fact (e.g. 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not with F/Z/Z-angle mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises.

Name the WHOLE before calculating line/point unknowns (180° on a line, 360° at a point) and sanity-check against it; but do NOT apply whole-minus-parts to a vertically opposite angle — it is found by equality.
Hold the two crossing relationships apart explicitly: vertically opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary; do not let pupils apply 'subtract from 180' to an opposite pair.
Tap-to-reveal / static diagrams introduce vocabulary only; they cannot set a problem or check a chained deduction and must not be the sole activity for the multi-step skill.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess isolated facts and the key trap; they do not elicit an independent multi-step chain with a stated reason at each step, which requires the construction task.

Live-recolouring, dragging rays and sliders are optional ways to make the equal/supplementary relationships visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and a physical hinged-stick model achieves the same demonstration.

The additive and equation-based steps rely on correct arithmetic: 180−130=50, 130−40=90, and 2x+10=130 ⇒ 2x=120 ⇒ x=60; check these when authoring items and do not offer wrong partial values as valid alternatives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

One cited source (National curriculum in England mathematics KS3) is marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activity 1 as an exact copy supporting the multi-step application principle; treat its claim as unconfirmed pending a fresh check and do not read it as verified evidence.

Fixed an over-generalisation: the original 'the unknown is the whole minus the known parts' was being applied to EVERY unknown; this is only valid for line/point angles, so the guidance now scopes subtraction to those cases and states that a vertically opposite angle is found by equality, preventing reinforcement of the subtract-from-180 misconception.

The original claims that a static image 'cannot' teach the skill and that a third dimension or a persona/conversation 'adds nothing' reflect catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (e.g. static diagrams are a vocabulary scaffold). No universal necessity of the interactive format is asserted.

Arithmetic independently checked and correct: opposite of 130° is 130°; adjacent 180−130=50°; split remainder 130−40=90°; 2x+10=130 gives x=60. No dubious alternative values were carried into learner items.

probeDeeper: Point to the angle opposite 130° and ask 'how do you KNOW it's 130 and not 50?' — forcing the equal-versus-supplementary distinction into a reason
'If I opened the crossing wider, what happens to this angle and to the one next to it?' — a dynamic counterexample separating opposite from adjacent
'The diagram isn't drawn to scale — why can you still be sure of your answer?' — pressing that the facts, not the picture, license the deduction
'You found this angle was 90° — where does that value come from, and what can you now work out with it?' — checking they can carry a result forward
assess.correctAnswer: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite equal); the two adjacent angles are 50° each (angles on a straight line sum to 180°). For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°. For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120, x = 60. Each step is justified by a named angle fact, not by measuring.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats vertically opposite angles as supplementary — subtracts from 180 to find the opposite angle ('they're next to each other so they add to 180')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the crossing as two relationships held apart — opposite EQUAL, adjacent supplementary — with the hinged-sticks model: as one angle opens, its opposite opens equally
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(c) gives 50° (or 180−value) for the angle vertically OPPOSITE the given one, instead of the equal value

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises that all four angles at a crossing are equal ('they're all made by the same two lines, so they're the same')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different; establish that only opposite pairs are equal, adjacent pairs sum to 180°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports all four angles as 130° (or all equal), ignoring the supplementary adjacent pair

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — treats a straight line as 360° or a point as 180° when setting up the calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the whole aloud before calculating — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point — and sanity-check the answer against it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts from the wrong total (e.g. 360−130 for an angle on a straight line), giving an out-of-range or impossible answer

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the first angle correctly but cannot chain — doesn't carry a found value into the next step, or makes an arithmetic slip mid-chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold by writing each found angle onto the diagram before the next step so it becomes a visible given; do not reteach the facts — the reasoning is sound, the chain just needs support
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets the first unknown right then stalls on (b), or the individual facts are right but the final chained value is wrong through a slip

responseLevels.gap: Cannot apply the facts reliably — treats vertically opposite as supplementary, uses the wrong whole, or measures the not-to-scale diagram; single angles come out wrong
responseLevels.full: Chains multiple facts to find several angles, naming the reason at each step, carries found values forward, and sets up and solves an equation for an unknown — transferring to a new configuration and justifying from structure not appearance
responseLevels.partial: Finds single angles using one fact each and can state the facts, but cannot chain them across the diagram, mis-handles the equation, or reverts to measuring — has the facts as isolated statements, not as tools that combine

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a NOT-TO-SCALE diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, plus a third ray splitting the angle opposite into two parts, one of which is marked 40°. Set them to: (a) find the three unmarked angles at the crossing and, for each, say the fact they used; (b) find the remaining part of the split angle; then (c) here two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130° — write and solve an equation for x. Watch whether they treat the opposite angle as equal or as 180 minus, whether they name a reason at each step, and whether they carry found angles forward rather than measuring the picture.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the facts gives 130° for the opposite angle and 50° for the adjacent, naming each; a child with the common error gives 50° for the OPPOSITE angle (treating it as supplementary) — a visibly different answer. The not-to-scale figure means a child who measures lands wrong, and the multi-step chain and the equation reveal whether the facts are merely recognised or can be applied and carried forward.
